files.text:
On the first of December 1944 the Mississippi River Commission at Vicksburg received a report from Harold Fisk, a geologist from Louisiana State University, on how the valley of the lower Mississippi had been made. Most of it is sections, borings and argument. At the back is a set of fifteen sheets, Plate 22, that follow the river down from Cape Girardeau in Missouri to Donaldsonville in Louisiana, and on them the river is drawn not once but twenty times. The present channel runs pale down each sheet between banks in heavy ink. Around it, overlapping like spilled ribbon, are the places it used to be: rose, straw, sage and sky blue, flat or hatched or stippled, each colour a stage, numbered from one, the oldest, to twenty, the river as it stood that year.

The last three stages Fisk could copy from surveys made in 1765, 1820 and 1880. The others he reconstructed from aerial photographs, in which an old channel shows through the fields as a curving band of darker soil and the banks of an old bend as faint concentric lines, and from borings that found the clay of vanished lakes beneath the cotton. Later geologists have redrawn his dates. The maps are still the ones people know.

A river on a flat plain cannot run straight for long. Where it bends, the water on the outside of the curve is thrown against the bank, faster and deeper, while a corkscrew current along the bed carries sand toward the inside. The outer bank is undercut and slumps in, a slab at a time, at high water; the sand is dropped where the current slackens on the inside of the bend, as a point bar. So every bend eats outward and builds inward at once, and because the hardest scour comes a little below the sharpest part of the turn, the whole loop leans and creeps down the valley. Each flood adds a low ridge along the inside bank, and the old ones stay behind it as ridge and swale, the growth rings of the bend.

A loop that grows long enough doubles back until only a neck of land divides it from its own course downstream. In some flood the water goes across the neck instead of around, and within days the river has a new channel. Sand settles in both mouths of the old loop, which is left as a crescent lake; over the centuries it fills with clay and turns to cypress swamp, then to a damp field with a curve in it. The clay is tougher than the sand around it, and when the river returns it bends around the old plug, which is why Fisk's channels buckle where they meet. Mark Twain, who had been a pilot on the river, counted its cut-offs and did the arithmetic:

In the space of one hundred and seventy-six years the Lower Mississippi has shortened itself two hundred and forty-two miles. That is an average of a trifle over one mile and a third per year. Therefore, any calm person, who is not blind or idiotic, can see that in the Old Oolitic Silurian Period, just a million years ago next November, the Lower Mississippi River was upwards of one million three hundred thousand miles long, and stuck out over the Gulf of Mexico like a fishing-rod. And by the same token any person can see that seven hundred and forty-two years from now the Lower Mississippi will be only a mile and three-quarters long, and Cairo and New Orleans will have joined their streets together, and be plodding comfortably along under a single mayor and a mutual board of aldermen. There is something fascinating about science. One gets such wholesale returns of conjecture out of such a trifling investment of fact.

The Corps of Engineers had less patience with the wandering. In 1831 Henry Shreve dug across the neck of Turnbull's Bend, above Baton Rouge, to shorten the trip for steamboats, and the river took his cut. The upper arm of the abandoned loop, Old River, became a short channel to the Atchafalaya, which offered the Mississippi a shorter and steeper way to the Gulf. In 1952 Fisk reported that the Atchafalaya was taking more of the flow every decade and would capture the river within a generation. The Corps' answer, finished in 1963, was the Old River Control Structure: gates that let the Atchafalaya have three tenths of the water and hold the rest in its bed past Baton Rouge and New Orleans. The flood of 1973 nearly tore it out of the ground. It holds, for now, and the river leans on it.

# meander A river seen from above wanders across its floodplain as you scroll, and the centuries pile up behind it in the manner of Harold Fisk's 1944 maps of the ancient courses of the lower Mississippi. The page starts as a printed survey sheet: a warm-grey base of township and section lines, section numbers, spot heights, bayous, swamp, a railroad and a few towns, and across it one river drawn as Fisk draws the modern one, quieter than the colours: the sheet's own buff inside, fine wavering banklines in warm ink, a dashed thalweg, levees with hachures either side, and M I S S I S S I P P I R I V E R in spaced capitals along the channel. As you scroll, its bends grow, lean and travel downstream; a few fine scroll lines mark the old inner banks; necks narrow until the river breaks through and a loop is left as an oxbow lake, which takes a name in italic, silts into a swamp of marsh tufts and ends as a scar. Each stage of the river is printed in its own Fisk tint when the next one begins: mostly flat, a few with a sparse screen, its line plate a hair out of register, the grey base printed over it all. Where a younger stage sweeps through an older one it destroys those deposits, so the older survives only as clipped fragments with crisp edges: Fisk's packed mosaic. Numerals (some circled) name the patches, and a legend fills in stage by stage. Scroll back and it all un-happens. With a mouse, pointing at an old course (or its swatch) makes the rest recede. ```html
``` Or call it yourself: ```js import { meander } from './meander.js'; const destroy = meander(el, { seed: 3, courses: 10, runway: 420 }); destroy.state(); // { step, frames, done, oxbows, orient, k, renderMs, rebuildMs, computeMs } destroy(); // canvas, legend, listeners, observers, timers ``` The section becomes a tall runway with the stage pinned inside it. The valley runs along the stage's longer side: left to right on a desktop, top to bottom on a phone, zoomed so the belt fills the width, with the legend in the margin under the map. ## Options On the element (`data-*`) or in the options object, which wins. | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-seed` | `seed` | `7` | the whole history is deterministic from it | | `data-courses` | `courses` | `13` | stages the history is divided into (2-14); the present river is one more | | `data-steps` | `steps` | `2600` | simulation steps scrubbed by the scroll (about 0.05 W of migration each at a sharp bend) | | `data-runway` | `runway` | `350` | section height in svh; the stage (100svh) is pinned for the rest | | `data-span` | `span` | `72` | channel widths of valley shown along the long side (smaller = closer) | | `data-hetero` | `hetero` | `.75` | how unevenly the plain erodes (0 = textbook sine-generated bends, 1 = ragged Fisk loops) | | `data-clay` | `clay` | `.4` | erodibility of an old oxbow's clay plug, relative to the sand around it | | `data-decay` | `decay` | `.9` | length (in W) of the upstream curvature kernel; longer = longer wavelength | | | `ymax`, `soft` | `14`, `8` | half-width of the meander belt in W, and how softly the bluffs push back | | | `cut` | `1.15` | centreline distance (W) at which a neck breaks | | | `lake`, `swamp` | `160`, `520` | steps until a lake starts to fill, and until it is only a scar | | | `L`, `ds`, `dt`, `omega`, `gamma`, `spin`, `smoothing`, `noise`, `force`, `gap` | | the simulation's own constants, see the top of the script | ## The real thing What a real observer of a lowland river would see (notes in the brief's spirit, from Leopold & Wolman, Ikeda-Parker-Sawai 1981, Howard & Knutson 1984, and Fisk's report): channel width W about a kilometre; meander wavelength 10-14 W; sinuosity rising toward 2-3 before neck cut-offs cap it; banks migrating a few per cent of W a year at the apex and not at all at the crossings; bends that grow, skew and translate downstream; the outer bank eroding while the inner one builds a point bar whose old shorelines survive as concentric ridge and swale; necks that close over decades and break in a single flood; oxbows whose ends plug with sand first, so the lake is a crescent with tapered horns, then fill with clay over centuries; a belt held between bluffs. What is modelled: - **Migration** (Howard & Knutson's form of the Ikeda-Parker-Sawai model). At each point the bank moves along the normal at `R1 = Ω·C + Γ·∫C(s-ξ)e^(-ξ/λ)dξ / ∫e^(-ξ/λ)dξ`, with Ω = -1, Γ = 2.5 and λ = 0.9 W, curvature C in 1/W. The local term straightens, the upstream-weighted term pushes outward, and because it lags the bend the greatest erosion falls just downstream of the apex: bends grow, lean and travel down-valley. The convolution is computed as a running exponential sum, so a step costs O(n). - **Resampling** to half a channel width each step, with a light Laplacian smoothing (8%). - **Neck cut-offs**: a spatial hash finds two points more than 9 W apart along the river and less than 1.15 W apart on the ground; the loop between them is removed and kept as an oxbow with its step. - **Erodibility** varies over the plain (smooth value noise, ±75%), and each oxbow leaves a clay plug that erodes at 0.4 of the rate, Fisk's own observation; this is what turns regular sine bends into the buckled, compound loops of his plates. The belt is soft-confined at ±14 W (bluffs). - **Bends from upstream**: the kernel at the inflow is fed by a slowly wandering curvature, standing for the meanders above the map; about 20 W at each end of the valley is simulated off screen so the ends never show. - **Scroll lines**: three or four per stage, at uneven moments, drawn along the bank that is building (the one the channel is moving away from, the sign of `R1`), only where it migrates noticeably, so they fan out round the apex and pinch out at the crossings. Simplified: no chute cut-offs, no avulsion, constant width and discharge, no sediment budget, no floods as events (each step is an average year or so), and the "courses" are equal slices of time rather than the river's own epochs. ## How it draws - **History first**: about 2600 steps are computed at load in 12 ms slices between frames (about 0.5 s in all on a laptop); every step's centreline is kept (around 6 MB). Scroll maps to a step, eased toward the target with a 0.14 s time constant so it settles. Nothing runs while the scroll is still. - **Ownership**: a grid at half a channel width records, for each place, the last stage whose channel swept it. At the close of each stage a chamfer distance transform finds roomy places for numerals; numerals stay put while their place stays theirs. The same grid answers the pointer. - **Three plates, as in print.** - *Paper* (base canvas): a faint buff and a still grain. - *Colours* (into the same base canvas, one stage at a time): the stage's swept ground (its centrelines every third step, stroked a channel wide) is first erased back to bare sheet with a hard edge (the river destroyed the older deposits there), then its tint plate (flat or sparsely screened, with grain) is multiplied over it, then its line plate (a faint outline, its scroll lines, the banks of its oxbow scars) is multiplied half a pixel or so out of register. Older stages survive as clipped fragments, each with its own numeral where there is room. Moving forward adds one stage; moving back rebuilds (about 5-20 ms). - *Grey base* (its own canvas, drawn once per size, multiplied over the colours every frame): the irregular survey grid (township rows with correction-line jogs, slightly skewed sections), small section numbers (mostly in the cells near the belt), spot heights, dotted contours, bayous (two named), swamp tufts, a railroad with its branch, towns. - **Each frame**: paper and colours; the stage just closed fading in from bare sheet; the current stage's fresh ground as bare sheet with pencil scroll lines; the grey base plate over all of it; numerals (hidden where fresh ground has covered them); lakes; levees (a hachured line each side of the present belt, from a dilated and smoothed envelope of the channel); the river; its name. About 2-5 ms of script per frame. - **The river's name**: each capital is set where the channel crosses an evenly spaced point down the valley, at the crossing that runs most down-valley, turned to the channel and kept upright. Each letter remembers the crossing it used last frame and strongly prefers it, so letters do not jump between crossings as you scrub (forgotten after a big jump). - **Lakes** are crescents whose horns plug and whose width narrows with age, the sheet's buff inside with a fine warm shoreline and one faint waterline while open, turning sage with marsh tufts, then dissolving into the scar already in the colours. The larger ones get a name from a list of real lower-Mississippi oxbow lakes (Lake Bruin, Lake St. John, Moon Lake, ...), set letter by letter along the straightest part of the open water, haloed in paper. ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--paper` | `#f3f0e8` | page colour (the highlight wash and the lake-name halo use it) | | `--ink`, `--ink-2` | `#141312`, `#4a4744` | legend rules and lettering | | `--mr-serif` | Cormorant Garamond | lake names, "Scale of Miles" | | `--mr-sans` | Inter | numerals and the legend | The course colours and screens are in `COURSES` at the top of the script, sampled from the legend of Plate 22, Sheet 7 (vermilion-salmon reds, yellowish greens, grey blues). `BASE_INK` the grey of the base plate, `TOWNS` and `BAYOUS` the names on it. ## Events (for sound later) | event | detail | when | |---|---|---| | `meander:cutoff` | `{ step, length }` (length in W) | the scroll carries the river through a neck cut-off (forward only) | | `meander:course` | `{ course }` | a stage closes and its colour is laid down (forward only) | Both bubble from the section. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - The canvas and legend are `aria-hidden`; give the section an `aria-label` (the demo does). The essay around it carries the content. - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: no runway and no pin; the finished map after the whole history, still. Pointing still highlights a course. - `touch-action: pan-y` on the stage; a vertical swipe always scrolls. - Without JS the stage shows a detail of Fisk's plate. ## Cost - One-time: ~0.5 s of simulation in slices (longer on a phone, during which the map shows the last computed step), ~6 MB of history. - Four canvases the size of the stage at DPR up to 2 (visible, colours, grey base, scratch), plus one more after the first hover. Base rebuilds only when scrolling back past a stage boundary. - No loop while still, off screen (IntersectionObserver) or in a hidden tab. ## Credits - Harold N. Fisk, *Ancient Courses, Mississippi River Meander Belt*, Plate 22, Sheet 7, from *Geological Investigation of the Alluvial Valley of the Lower Mississippi River* (Mississippi River Commission, 1944); public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Details in `assets/credits.json`. - Mark Twain, *Life on the Mississippi* (1883), chapter 17, quoted in the demo. - Migration law after Ikeda, Parker & Sawai (1981) and Howard & Knutson (1984); the running-sum kernel and cut-off test follow the approach of Zoltán Sylvester's meanderpy, reimplemented. No third-party code.
